title: After
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 28 of 40
content:
The morning after our first kiss, Severus Snape became aggressively professional.

He called me “Consultant” three times before breakfast.

The first was irritating.

The second was funny.

By the third, I understood he was terrified.

“Consultant,” he said, holding out the Ministry file, “you will need this.”

I took it.

“Thank you, Professor.”

His eyes narrowed.

“Not currently.”

“Neither am I a consultant until nine.”

“It is eight forty-seven.”

“Then stop flirting with my job title.”

His mouth opened.

Closed.

I smiled.

“Cruel,” he said.

“You survived.”

He looked away before I could see whether he smiled.

We were leaving for the Ministry at nine thirty.

The castle seemed offensively normal. Students ate porridge. Owls arrived. Someone dropped a goblet. No trumpet announced that Severus Snape had kissed me in a storeroom between nettles and unicorn horn.

I was grateful.

I was also disappointed, which was ridiculous.

Snape ate almost nothing.

I pushed toast toward him.

He pushed it back.

“Not today.”

“You need food.”

“I need not to vomit during testimony.”

“That is a fair point.”

He looked at me as if expecting argument.

“See?” I said. “I can be reasonable.”

“Disturbing.”

Beneath the table, his knee touched mine.

Neither of us moved it.

That tiny contact steadied us more than conversation.

McGonagall caught us at the end of breakfast with a small envelope and the expression she reserved for students who were old enough to know better.

“The Ministry has changed the witness entrance,” she told Severus. “Reporters have been gathering at the public lifts.”

He reached for the envelope. She kept hold of it until he looked up.

“Severus. I am telling you because you deserve the choice, not because I am instructing you to hide.”

His face hardened. “A distinction with which I am not entirely unfamiliar.”

“I know,” she said. “And I should have made it more often.”

I pretended to study the breakfast menu while both of them stood with years of unfinished history between their hands. The porridge had gone cold. Somewhere down the table a student laughed at a joke that had nothing to do with war.

When she left, I asked whether he wanted me beside him at the public entrance.

“You need not place yourself before cameras on my account.”

“That's not what I asked.”

“No,” he said, looking annoyed with himself. “It is not.”

I had told him I was ethically non-monogamous and preferred polyamory; I had never offered to make him a secret, and I had never asked him to be a public exhibit either.

“If we walk in together, people may invent things,” I said. “If we walk separately, they'll invent different things. Which choice do you actually want?”

He put the envelope on the table and considered it as though it contained a difficult examination problem.

“The witness entrance,” he said at last. “Because I want testimony heard before gossip. Not because I am ashamed of your company.”

“And after?”

His gaze met mine. “After, you may have the satisfaction of being seen leaving with an exceptionally disagreeable man.”

“It's a date, then.”

“It is a logistical arrangement.”

“That too.”


After breakfast, we returned to the dungeon for our coats.

The storeroom door was closed.

I looked at it.

Snape caught me.

“No.”

“What?”

“Whatever expression you are making.”

“I am looking at a door.”

“You are looking at it sentimentally.”

“I didn't know that was possible.”

“With you, apparently anything is.”

I turned toward him.

“Are you regretting it?”

The question removed the humor.

Snape went still.

“No.”

Immediate.

Certain.

Relief warmed me.

“Are you?” he asked.

“No.”

His shoulders lowered by a fraction.

“Good.”

I stepped closer.

“We don't have to decide what it means today.”

He studied me.

“You enjoy postponing definitions.”

“I enjoy not turning one kiss into a legal proceeding before the actual legal proceeding.”

“That is almost sensible.”

“Thank you.”

“I said almost.”

His hand found mine.

I smiled.

“We can do this,” I said.

“The hearing?”

“Yes.”

He looked down at our hands.

“And this?”

My heart stumbled.

“Yes.”

Snape's thumb moved over my knuckles.

“You cannot know that.”

“No. Neither can you.”

His eyes lifted.

“But I want to try.”

A long pause.

“So do I,” he said.

That was enough.

The Ministry atrium was worse than I expected.

Reporters crowded behind a barrier. Cameras flashed. Quills wrote without hands. Snape went rigid the instant we stepped from the Floo.

His hand left mine.

Not rejection.

Protection.

The gesture still hurt.

He saw it.

“Not here,” he murmured.

I nodded.

“Okay.”

His eyes searched my face.

“You understand?”

“Yes.”

The public did not get this yet.

Maybe ever.

It was ours before it became anyone else's story.

A reporter shouted, “Professor Snape, do you expect acquittal?”

Another: “Were you romantically obsessed with Lily Potter?”

Snape stopped.

I felt the temperature drop around him.

The second reporter raised a Quick-Quotes Quill.

“Is it true your Patronus remained hers because you could never love anyone else?”

My stomach twisted.

Not jealousy.

Fury.

They had turned a dead woman and a living man's grief into entertainment.

Snape's face became blank.

He began walking again.

I followed.

The reporter called after us, “Do you think Lily Potter would forgive you?”

Snape faltered.

One step.

Barely.

I moved beside him.

Not touching.

Just there.

He kept walking.

Inside the lift, the doors closed.

The silence was immediate.

Snape stared at the brass numbers above us.

“I hate them,” I said.

His mouth twitched.

“How refreshingly nuanced.”

“I contain multitudes.”

“Apparently.”

The lift descended.

“I wanted to hex him,” I admitted.

“Which one?”

“The one who asked about Lily.”

“That narrows nothing.”

I laughed despite myself.

Then Snape said, “Thank you for not.”

“For your sake or mine?”

“Both.”

The hearing chamber waited below.

Before the doors opened, Snape turned toward me.

His face was pale.

“After,” he said.

I understood.

After the hearing.

After the testimony.

After whatever judgment came.

We would return to this.

To us.

I held his gaze.

“After,” I agreed.

The doors opened.

We stepped out separately.

It did not feel like distance.

It felt like a promise.\n\nThe lift stopped two floors below the hearing chamber.\n\nA witch from the Department of Magical Law Enforcement stepped inside carrying three folders and the exhausted expression of someone who had spent the morning being shouted at by people with inherited seats. She recognized Snape immediately.\n\nHer eyes widened.\n\nThen, to her credit, she looked at the floor numbers instead of staring.\n\nSnape became so still beside me that I could feel the effort of it.\n\nI did not reach for his hand. Not because I did not want to. Because he had chosen distance in the atrium, and I wanted that choice to remain his instead of becoming something he had to defend.\n\nThe witch got off one floor later.\n\nThe doors closed.\n\nSnape exhaled.\n\n“You are thinking very loudly,” he said.\n\n“I thought that was your specialty.”\n\n“Yours is more obvious.”\n\nI looked at him. “Do you want me farther away?”\n\nHis head turned sharply.\n\n“No.”\n\n“Closer?”\n\nHe glanced at the brass doors, as though the Ministry itself might file a report on the answer.\n\n“Not here.”\n\n“Okay.”\n\nThat was all.\n\nNo punishment. No sulking. No test hidden inside the question.\n\nThe lift continued upward.\n\nSnape stared at the numbers changing over the door. “You make boundaries sound offensively simple.”\n\n“They are simple.”\n\n“They are not easy.”\n\n“No.” I shifted the file under my arm. “Those are different things.”\n\nHe considered that.\n\nThe doors opened onto a quieter corridor. A clerk waited beside a carved oak door with a clipboard. Beyond the windows, London was gray with rain.\n\n“Mr. Snape,” she said. “They are nearly ready.”\n\n“Of course they are.”\n\n“You may wait here.”\n\nShe indicated a bench.\n\nSnape looked at it as though the Ministry had provided a personal insult with cushions.\n\nI sat.\n\nAfter a moment, he sat beside me.\n\nNot touching.\n\nClose enough that the sleeve of his robe brushed mine when either of us breathed too deeply.\n\nWe waited.\n\nA clock ticked at the far end of the corridor. Papers rustled behind the hearing-room door. Somewhere nearby, a man argued in a whisper about procedural authority.\n\nSnape's fingers tapped once against his knee. Stopped. Began again.\n\nI opened the Ministry file and pretended to read.\n\n“Page twelve,” he said.\n\n“What?”\n\n“If you intend to pretend you are occupied, page twelve contains enough bureaucratic nonsense to justify your expression.”\n\nI turned to page twelve.\n\nHe was right.\n\n“This sentence has four semicolons.”\n\n“Criminal.”\n\n“Should we report it?”\n\n“After the hearing.”\n\nThe words landed between us.\n\nAfter.\n\nNot if.\n\nI closed the file.\n\nThe clerk opened the door. “Mr. Snape?”\n\nHe stood.\n\nFor one second his hand hovered near mine.\n\nThen his fingers touched the back of my wrist—briefly, deliberately, hidden by the fall of our sleeves.\n\nIt was not a kiss.\n\nIt was not a declaration.\n\nIt was enough to tell me he remembered the promise.\n\nAfter.\n\nI followed him into the chamber.
